This document covers two main topics:

#### I. Why visualize data?
#### II. Golden Rules of Data Visualization

# I. Why visualize data?
A classic example of why data visualization is not just useful but also *important* uses data generated by F.J. Anscombe (1973). From these data, we can see how four different data sets can have the same summary statistics, yet look very different when plotted.

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = '/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170')
```

Here, we can just load the tidyverse package, which simultaneously loads several of the packages we will be using, including ggplot2, dplyr, and tidyr. We will also need a few additional packages.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggalt)
library(gapminder)
```

The **Anscombe data** are included in base R, and can be viewed simply by typing the name, anscombe:
```{r}
anscombe
```

We can reorder the data so the x's & y's for the four datasets can be viewed next to each other
```{r}
anscombereorder <- anscombe[, c(1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8)]
anscombereorder
```

Next, we will convert these data to "long" format for analysis within the ggplot function and visualization. We can do this using functions within base R, or using the pivot_longer() function that is part of the tidyr package:
```{r}
#convert these data to long format
anscombelong <- data.frame(x = unlist(anscombe[, 1:4]), y = unlist(anscombe[,5:8]), dataset = rep(1:4, each = 11))

#The pivot_longer() or gather() functions in tidyr also work 
alt_long<-anscombe %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c(".value", "dataset"),
               names_pattern = "(.)(.)"
  )

print(head(anscombelong)) #base R data manipulation
print(head(as.data.frame(alt_long))) #tidyr data manipulation
```

Next, we summarize the data using dplyr. Note the identical values for each dataset!!
```{r, message = FALSE}
sum_ans<-anscombelong %>% group_by(dataset) %>% summarise(`x-mean` = mean(x),`y-mean` = mean(y), `x-variance` = var(x), `y-variance` = var(y), `correlation-xy` = cor(x,y))

as.data.frame(sum_ans)
```

Lastly, we will plot the data, including the regression line formula and r-squared values. Here we will use a function that is not built into base R or any of our installed packages, so we'll run it first so that it works in our plot function that follows.
```{r}
#Use the function below to plot the line and r^2 on the figures shown below
lm_eqn <- function(df){
  m <- lm(y ~ x, df);
  eq <- substitute(italic(y) == a + b %.% italic(x)*","~~italic(r)^2~"="~r2, 
                   list(a = format(coef(m)[[1]], digits = 2), 
                        b = format(coef(m)[[2]], digits = 2), 
                        r2 = format(summary(m)$r.squared, digits = 3)))
  as.character(as.expression(eq))                
}
```

Now we can plot the data. Here I'm calling the figure to an object, anscombe_plots, so that I can easily save it to file using the ggsave() function below.
```{r, message = FALSE}
#plot the data
anscombe_plots<-
  ggplot(anscombelong, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",se = FALSE) + 
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 4, label = lm_eqn(anscombelong), 
           color = "black", parse = TRUE) + 
  ylim(3, 13) + xlim(4,19) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  theme_bw()

anscombe_plots
```

Save the plot using ggsave():
```{r, message = FALSE}
ggsave("Week6/ansc_pl.pdf",plot = anscombe_plots)
```


#### Additional example: Data patterns behind a correlation coefficient of 0, 0.5, and 0.9

From https://janhove.github.io/teaching/2016/11/21/what-correlations-look-like
```{r}
source("http://janhove.github.io/RCode/plot_r.R")
plot_r(r = 0, n = 50)
plot_r(r = 0.5, n = 50)
plot_r(r = 0.9, n = 50)
```

# II. Golden Rules of Data Visualization

Note, several examples presented were pulled *directly* from Kieran Healy's "Data Visualization - A Practical Introduction". The entire text is available online here: https://socviz.co/index.html.
Please use it to your advantage and find many more figure examples within!!

![](/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Fall2020/Week11/images/dv-cover-pupress.jpg)

## 1. Choose the right chart type
![](/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Week6/charttype.png)

## 2. Consider interpretability
![The figure above shows the increase in human error in estimating plot values based on position and size of values within different chart types (by length, area, or angle).](/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Fall2020/Week11/images/interpretability.png)

Take home: When it comes to interpretation, typically, bar charts > stacked charts > area-based charts... 
But there are definitely exceptions -- use your good judgment!

## 3. Use appropriate point/line sizes, and emphasize areas of importance as needed
```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
leaddat<-read.csv("/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Fall2020/Week9/PhillyLeadCensusTract.csv")

p<-ggplot(data = leaddat, aes(x = MedianHHincome, y = perc_5plus)) 

p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple",size=0.2) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue",size=0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") +
#center title using theme() and element_text() command below
  ggtitle("Points and line are too small!!")+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
  
p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple",size=7) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") +
  ggtitle("Points are too BIG!!") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple",size=1.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue",size=1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") +
  ggtitle("Points and line nicely sized!") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

We can also add text and shapes to our figure to highlight specific parts of the data or make the figure easier to interpret. Here we'll use an organ donor dataset.

* geom_text() = can be used to include data labels within figure
```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
organdata<-read.csv("Week6/organdata.csv")

by_country <- organdata %>% group_by(consent_law, country) %>%
    summarize_if(is.numeric, funs(mean, sd), na.rm = TRUE) %>%
    ungroup()

#the geom_text_repel() function in the ggprepel library offsets the label from positioning directly over the point; replace with geom_text() for comparison
p <- ggplot(data = by_country,
            mapping = aes(x = gdp_mean, y = health_mean))

p + geom_point() +
    geom_text_repel(aes(label = country)) +
    ggtitle("Label all countries") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p + geom_point() +
    geom_text_repel(data = subset(by_country, gdp_mean > 25000),
                    mapping = aes(label = country)) +
    ggtitle("Label only countries with mean GDP > 25000") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

#Use the "or" operator, |, to subset on multiple possible values
#Note the "and" operator, &, is another option not shown here
p + geom_point() +
    geom_text_repel(data = subset(by_country, gdp_mean > 25000 | health_mean < 1500 | country %in% "Belgium"), mapping = aes(label = country)) +
    ggtitle("Label only countries with mean GDP > 25000 \n or mean(health) < 1500 or name = Germany") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

* geom_encircle() = to draw a line around points (ggalt library)
```{r}
p <- ggplot(data = by_country,
            mapping = aes(x = gdp_mean, y = health_mean))

p + geom_point() +
    geom_encircle(data = subset(by_country, health_mean > 2500), color = "red") +
    ggtitle("Circle countries with mean GDP > 25000") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

* annotate() = add shapes and or text to specific figure locations
```{r}
p <- ggplot(data = organdata,
            mapping = aes(x = roads, y = donors))

p + geom_point() +
    annotate(geom = "rect", xmin = 125, xmax = 155,
             ymin = 30, ymax = 35, fill = "red", alpha = 0.2) + 
    annotate(geom = "text", x = 157, y = 33, label = "A surprisingly high \n recovery rate!", hjust = 0)

```

## 4. Use appropriate color combinations; don't use too many colors, aim for 3-5 colors max
![Normal color vision and the visible color specturm for three different types of colorblindness; Deutran is the most common type of colorblindness.](/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Fall2020/Week11/images/colorblind.png)
## 5. Include axis labels and title as needed
- Use appropriate font sizes!!
- Write the title out as a result, i.e., similar to a newspaper headline

Change font size, type and style (e.g., italics, bold) using the 'size', 'face' and 'family' arguments. 
```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
p<-ggplot(data = leaddat, aes(x = MedianHHincome, y = perc_5plus)) 

p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") +
  ggtitle("Change font family, size, and style in axes and tick-mark values") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 10, face = "bold")) +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12, family = "Times")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 20)) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic", size = 20))
```

This is a *terrible* looking figure! But we sure have figured out how to make a lot of text alternations!

## 6. Don't overdo it; maximize data:ink or data:junk ratio
![A classic junk chart!](/Users/brown8lm/Dropbox/ENVS_DataScience/courses/ENV170/Fall2020/Week11/images/chartjunk.png)
Is the legend in the above figure very useful? Is the shadow behind the bars necessary? Does the 3D visual add any value or meaning?

Below we can remove various elements of the ggplot default background:
```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") + 
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") + 
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Remove gray background but keep gridlines") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p + 
  geom_point(color = "purple") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue") + 
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) + 
  ylab("Blood lead level ≥5 µg/dL") + 
  xlab("Median household income") + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(panel.border = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.line = element_line(colour = "black")) +
  ggtitle("Remove all elements of background and box around figure") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

## 7. Always ask: 
- Is the visualization honest? 
- Is it meaningful? 
- Does it speak for itself?

Even inadvertently misleading is still being misleading...

A good figure should contain meaningful information that tells a valuable story, and ideally, should not need any additional accompany text beyond the data contained within the figure, the axis tick-mark values and labels, and the title if included. 
Note: It is not always necessary to include a title, only if it adds important and otherwise missing data, meaning, and value!

## 8. There aren't always hard and fast rules
In the two figures below, is one version clearly superior to the other? Is it a matter of opinion or of what we wish to emphasize about the data? How does one walk the line between emphasizing specific patterns or differences and being misleading?
